_readme: Cited facts behind live/cheatsheets.html. One rule governs this file: every bullet
carries a cite that points at the module section or glossary entry it came from. A
bullet without a cite does not belong here, for the same reason a flashcard without
a source does not belong in flashcards.html.
Paths are relative to live/cheatsheets.html, which is also where the fetch happens.
Numbers are copied from the module that derives them - never restated from memory,
and never rounded into something the module does not say.
Adding a sheet: append to clusters or modules, keep the track id in sync with
docs/BRAND.md track colours, and re-run check_links.py after wiring any new href.

tracks.title: GPU Programming
tracks.owns: Writing kernels that are correct first and fast second, on both HIP and CUDA, plus the portable Triton path.
tracks.prereq: C or C++ that you can read and modify. No GPU experience is assumed at A01.

bullets.text: The host/device split is the whole programming model: copy in, launch a grid, copy out. Every thread computes its own global index and works on its slice.
Every runtime call is checked and every kernel launch is followed by an error check. A silent launch failure looks exactly like a wrong answer.
Track A ends at A10 (CuTe, CUTLASS, cuTile), which is NVIDIA-only and marked optional. Everything before it runs on both vendors.

tracks.title: GPU + ML Performance
tracks.owns: Deciding what is actually limiting a workload, and proving it with a measurement rather than a guess.
tracks.prereq: Track A through A06. You need to have written a kernel before profiling one is meaningful.

bullets.text: The roofline comes first and the profiler second: form a hypothesis from intensity, then take the cheapest measurement that could kill it.
Almost every kernel in ML sits left of the ridge point, which is why fusing pays and why faster arithmetic often changes nothing.
Published ceilings are a starting point, not an answer. B02's lab derives peak FLOP/s and bandwidth from your own hardware.

tracks.title: ML System Design
tracks.owns: The design interview and the production system behind it: framing, data, training, serving, monitoring.
tracks.prereq: None technically. There is no GPU code in this track; its tools are standard-library Python.

bullets.text: An ML system exists to produce a decision, not a prediction. The first question is what action the system takes, never what model to use.
Model architecture is usually the least leveraged variable. The data pipeline is the system, and label leakage plus training-serving skew dominate its failure modes.
Design is constraint arithmetic: business goal, latency budget, traffic forecast and price list must be simultaneously satisfiable, and you should know which you would break first.

tracks.title: Distributed Computing
tracks.owns: The layer below ML: what it costs to talk between processes, over what wire, in what shape of cluster.
tracks.prereq: Track A basics. B07 and C03 already own sharding and fault tolerance, so Track D deliberately sits underneath them.

bullets.text: Adding processors adds capacity, not speed. You convert capacity into speed only to the extent the work is independent.
Every byte travels in one of a handful of tiers separated by roughly an order of magnitude each, and that ladder explains most placement decisions.
Every inter-node figure in this track is an analytic model and says so in its own output banner. No multi-node measurement exists in this repo.

clusters.title: Memory hierarchy and coalescing
clusters.sub: Why the same arithmetic runs at 15% or 70% of the ceiling

bullets.text: The hierarchy is registers, then shared memory / LDS, then L1 and L2, then global HBM. Each step down is roughly an order of magnitude slower and larger.
A cache line is fetched whole whether you use all of it or one byte of it. Stride-1 across a wavefront is one transaction; stride-8 is eight, and seven eighths of each is discarded.
Even a stride-1 access that starts misaligned can straddle two lines, so alignment is a separate concern from stride.
Staging through shared memory converts a strided global pattern into a coalesced one. A transpose goes from about 15% of the copy ceiling to about 70%.
Shared memory is banked, so the padding trick exists to break the conflict a naturally sized tile creates. Padding costs a column and buys back the conflict-free access.

clusters.title: Execution model, divergence and occupancy
clusters.sub: What the hardware executes, as opposed to what you wrote

bullets.text: A block is how you organize threads; a warp (32 lanes, NVIDIA) or wavefront (64 lanes, AMD CDNA) is how the hardware executes them. Size blocks as a multiple of the wider one for portability.

A branch that divides lanes within a wavefront executes both sides in turn, so the cost is the sum of the paths, not the max. A branch that is uniform across the wavefront skips the untaken side entirely.
Occupancy is a means, not a goal. More resident waves hide latency, but a kernel that is already bandwidth-saturated gains nothing from raising it.
warpSize stopped being constexpr in ROCm 7.0, and __AMDGCN_WAVEFRONT_SIZE__ is deprecated. A03 documents the portable form.

clusters.title: Fusion, online softmax and FlashAttention
clusters.sub: The intermediate you never store is the one you never move

bullets.text: Naive softmax overflows: expf(100) is +inf in fp32, so one large score turns a whole row into nan. Subtracting the row maximum is mathematically identical and numerically safe.
The online recurrence computes the running max and the running sum in one pass, which is what makes the safe version free rather than an extra pass over memory.
Unfused attention crosses the HBM boundary four times with an N-by-N payload. Fused traffic is 8Nd bytes against 8Nd + 8N^2, so the ratio is 1 + N/d: 9x at N=1k, 33x at 4k, 129x at 16k.
The dtype cancels out of that ratio. Moving to fp8 halves both sides and changes nothing about whether you should fuse.
Attention is not intrinsically memory-bound; unfused attention is. Fused intensity is N/2 and unbounded, while unfused saturates at d/2 forever.

clusters.title: Roofline and profiling
clusters.sub: Hypothesis first, then the cheapest measurement that could kill it

bullets.text: Attainable performance is min(peak FLOP/s, intensity x bandwidth). The ridge point is peak divided by bandwidth: the intensity at which you stop being bandwidth-limited.
Timeline tracing and kernel profiling answer different questions and are not interchangeable. Start with the timeline: the kernel is often a rounding error in the wall clock.
rocprofv3 now defaults to rocpd SQLite output rather than CSV, so pass --output-format csv explicitly if you want to read it with the usual tools.
Omniperf and Omnitrace were renamed in ROCm 6.3 to rocprof-compute and rocprof-sys-*. Older tutorials will name binaries that no longer exist.
A01's profiled run puts a 44 microsecond kernel inside a 72 millisecond program: 0.06% of the wall clock. Optimizing the kernel first would have been wasted effort.

clusters.title: Precision, numerics and quantization
clusters.sub: Exponent bits buy range, mantissa bits buy precision

bullets.text: That one sentence explains every format. bf16 keeps fp32's 8 exponent bits and cuts the mantissa to 7, so it has fp32's range with coarser steps and needs no loss scaling.
There are two incompatible fp8 formats. CDNA 3 (gfx942) implements FNUZ with exponent bias 8 and max 240; Hopper implements OCP with bias 7 and max 448.
The same bits decode about 2x apart between them, and 0x80 is NaN under FNUZ but negative zero under OCP. Moving a checkpoint between vendors is not a reinterpret-cast.
Quantization is a decode-side win: decode throughput is bandwidth over model bytes, so halving the weights nearly doubles it. Prefill barely notices.

clusters.title: Prefill, decode and serving throughput
clusters.sub: The same weights and kernel, two completely different machines

bullets.text: A transformer layer is about 12d^2 parameters at the usual FFN multiplier of 4, a forward pass costs about 2x params in FLOPs per token, and training about 6x. Those plus the KV-cache size are the whole envelope.
Arithmetic intensity of one projection is Td/(d + 2T). At d=4096 that is 1.0 at T=1, 62.1 at T=64, and 1024 at T=2048.
For small T the intensity is approximately T, so the batch size at which decode becomes compute-bound is roughly the machine's ridge point: 281 tokens against MI300X's 247 FLOP/byte.
This is why batching transforms decode and does almost nothing for prefill, and why a vendor quoting a FLOPs improvement is advertising a prefill number.
You do not optimize latency or throughput. You fix an SLO and maximize goodput: requests served within it.

clusters.title: Framing, metrics and data
clusters.sub: The two failure modes that dominate everything else

bullets.text: Define the decision before the prediction. Metrics are proxies for a business outcome, and the operating threshold comes from the relative cost of the two error types.
Label leakage puts information into training that will not exist at prediction time, which makes the offline metric a fiction rather than an overestimate.
Training-serving skew is the same feature computed two different ways in two different code paths. The fix is one path, not two paths kept in sync.

clusters.title: Optimization and deployment
clusters.sub: Cheapest and least risky fix first

bullets.text: The ordering is: do not call the model at all (caching, cascades, early exit), then serve it better (batching, runtime, graph capture), then shrink the numbers, then shrink the model.
Choose the serving pattern from latency, cost, freshness, connectivity and privacy requirements, not from habit. Online, async, streaming, batch and edge are genuinely different systems.
Scale on queue depth, not CPU or GPU utilization. A GPU can read as busy while the queue is empty, and as idle while requests are waiting.
The capstone works two designs end to end, LLM serving and a recommender, so the constraint arithmetic is practised rather than described.

clusters.title: Training systems, monitoring and drift
clusters.sub: A model can be perfectly healthy and quietly wrong

bullets.text: A training run at scale is a distributed system with a loss function attached. Its uptime depends on the input pipeline, bit-exact checkpoint resume, and how fast a dead rank is detected.
Monitor four layers - system, data, model, business - and alert on very few of them. Alerting on all four produces noise that trains people to ignore it.
Distinguish covariate shift (P(x) moved) from prior or label shift (P(y) moved). They have different causes and different fixes.

clusters.title: Scaling limits and cluster shape
clusters.sub: Amdahl bounds you from above; communication bends the curve back down

bullets.text: Amdahl says a fixed problem with serial fraction s can never exceed 1/s speedup. Gustafson says a growing problem escapes that, because the serial part does not grow with it.
Neither law includes communication. Add the alpha-beta term and the speedup curve does not plateau, it turns over: past some rank count you go slower.
A cluster is a shape, not a link. Diameter sets the latency term and bisection bandwidth sets the throughput term, and the shape decides which links you may use at once.
Memorize the identity: all-reduce = reduce-scatter + all-gather. Most of ZeRO and most of the tensor-parallel tricks are that identity applied somewhere.
Ring all-reduce moves 2(P-1)/P x S bytes per rank, which converges to 2S rather than P x S. Volume is essentially independent of rank count, which is why it replaced parameter servers.
The step count is linear though: 2(P-1) is 14 steps at 8 ranks and 2,046 at 1024. Volume converges, latency does not.
The latency/bandwidth crossover is S* = P x alpha x B. At P=8, alpha=8us, B=50 GB/s that is 3.05 MiB: below it you are paying for launches, not wire.
Mixed-precision Adam costs 16 bytes per parameter of resident state before any activation exists, so a 70B model needs about 1043 GiB on hardware with 192 GiB per device.

clusters.title: Interconnects, RDMA and real systems
clusters.sub: The tiers are an order of magnitude apart, and that is the whole subject

bullets.text: The ladder runs on-package memory, then scale-up links inside a node, then PCIe, then the scale-out network, then storage. Each tier is roughly 10x the one above it in cost per byte.
That ladder is why tensor parallelism is confined to one node: its per-layer all-reduce would cross the scale-out tier several times per layer otherwise.
algbw and busbw are not the same number. busbw scales algbw by the collective's ring factor, and comparing the wrong one across collectives is a common error.
Frontier, El Capitan, Aurora, Fugaku, Summit and LUMI differ enormously in processors and hardly at all in reasoning: each spends its design budget on moving data.

modules.title: Foundations and programming model
modules.one_liner: Copy in, launch a grid, copy out - and every thread finds its own slice by index.

bullets.text: The three-step model is the whole API surface at this level: host-to-device copy, kernel launch, device-to-host copy.
A profiled run here shows a 44 microsecond kernel inside a 72 millisecond program, which is 0.06% of the wall clock.

modules.title: Memory hierarchy and coalescing
modules.one_liner: A pyramid of memories, and a cache line that is fetched whole whether you use it or not.

bullets.text: Coalesced stride-1 access across a wavefront is one transaction; stride-8 is eight, with seven eighths of each line discarded.
Staging a transpose through shared memory with padding takes it from about 15% to about 70% of the copy ceiling.

modules.title: Execution model, occupancy and divergence
modules.one_liner: Blocks are yours; warps of 32 and wavefronts of 64 are the hardware's.

bullets.text: A divergent branch runs both sides in turn, so its cost is the sum of the paths. A wavefront-uniform branch skips the untaken side.
Occupancy hides latency; it does not create bandwidth. A saturated kernel gains nothing from more resident waves.

modules.title: Parallel reduction
modules.one_liner: Same N-1 additions, log2(N) levels instead of N-1 - depth is what the tree buys.

bullets.text: 16.7 million numbers finish in 24 levels rather than 16.7 million dependent steps.
The tree idles the array as it collapses: at 16 lanes only 15 of 64 lane-slots do work. Stage 7's algorithm cascade is what recovers that.
The nine-stage ladder is nine implementations of one function. Every stage must pass; a failing stage is a bug, not a rounding effect.

modules.title: Parallel scan and prefix sum
modules.one_liner: Looks irreducibly sequential; is not, because addition is associative.

bullets.text: Hillis-Steele is simple with O(n log n) work and O(log n) depth; Blelloch is work-efficient at O(n) with two passes.

modules.title: Tiled matrix multiply
modules.one_liner: The FLOPs are fixed; the bytes are a design choice.

bullets.text: Naive GEMM has intensity 0.25 FLOP/byte regardless of N. Tiling makes it T/4, so intensity scales with the tile.
At N=4096 fp32 that is 549.8 GB of traffic naive against 17.2 GB at T=32, to move matrices that occupy 201 MB.
Register blocking breaks the threads = T^2 constraint, giving a 64x64 tile from 256 threads instead of an illegal 4096.

modules.title: Softmax and fused kernels
modules.one_liner: Fix the overflow and win the extra pass at the same time.

bullets.text: expf(100) is +inf in fp32, so one large score turns an entire row into nan. Subtracting the row max is identical mathematically and safe numerically.
The online recurrence carries the running max and running sum together, so the safe version costs one pass rather than two.

modules.title: Triton foundations
modules.one_liner: Raise the unit of programming from one thread to one block of elements.

bullets.text: You write what a program does to a block-shaped slab; the compiler decides the thread mapping. That is the whole idea.

modules.title: Advanced Triton and FlashAttention
modules.one_liner: The score matrix you never store is the one you never move.

bullets.text: Unfused traffic is 8Nd + 8N^2, fused is 8Nd, so the ratio is 1 + N/d and the dtype cancels entirely.
The fused result is exact, not an approximation. It is the same answer with a different traffic profile.

modules.title: CuTe, CUTLASS and cuTile
modules.one_liner: NVIDIA-only and optional: what it takes to actually reach peak.

bullets.text: Peak needs tensor cores plus deep software pipelining, which is more machinery than a hand-written tiled GEMM contains.
Marked optional because it is NVIDIA-only. The AMD counterpart is Composable Kernel, named in the module.

modules.title: Accelerator architecture
modules.one_liner: A factory floor with a knowable structure, not a big pile of cores.

bullets.text: Hundreds of near-identical execution engines: AMD calls them CUs, NVIDIA calls them SMs, and the scheduling unit differs by vendor.
AMD's own CDNA 3 whitepaper and its Hot Chips 2024 slides disagree on Infinity Cache bandwidth (17.2 vs 14.7 TB/s). The module reports both rather than picking one.

modules.title: Roofline and arithmetic intensity
modules.one_liner: One formula: min(peak, intensity x bandwidth).

bullets.text: The ridge point is peak FLOP/s divided by peak bandwidth. Left of it you are bandwidth-bound no matter how good your arithmetic is.
Every kernel this curriculum writes plots left of the ridge, which is the argument for fusion in one picture.

modules.title: Profiling and bottleneck analysis
modules.one_liner: A decision procedure, not a command you run.

bullets.text: Form the hypothesis from the roofline, then take the cheapest measurement that could kill it.
Timeline tracing and kernel profiling are two levels and are not interchangeable. Start with the timeline.
rocprofv3 defaults to rocpd SQLite; pass --output-format csv if you want CSV.

modules.title: Precision and quantization
modules.one_liner: Exponent bits buy range; mantissa bits buy precision - fp32, bf16, fp16 and fp8 in one sentence.

bullets.text: bf16 keeps fp32's 8 exponent bits with a 7-bit mantissa, which is why it needs no loss scaling.
The two fp8 formats are not interchangeable: FNUZ on CDNA 3 and OCP on Hopper decode the same bits about 2x apart, and disagree on what 0x80 means.

modules.title: Transformer performance
modules.one_liner: Shrink the token count to 1 and the machine changes character.

bullets.text: About 12d^2 parameters per layer, about 2x params FLOPs per token forward, 6x for training.
Intensity is Td/(d+2T): 1.0 at T=1, 247 at T=281, 1024 at T=2048 when d=4096.
Decode at batch 1 uses about 0.4% of the machine's arithmetic. The cost is entirely the weight read.

modules.title: Inference serving optimizations
modules.one_liner: Fix an SLO, then maximize goodput - not latency, not throughput.

bullets.text: Batching raises tokens/s and raises every user's latency, so the two goals genuinely fight and you must pick the constraint.
Continuous batching admits and retires requests mid-flight rather than at batch boundaries, which is where most of the win is.

modules.title: Distributed training and sharding
modules.one_liner: 16 bytes per parameter of Adam state, before a single activation exists.

bullets.text: A 70B model needs about 1043 GiB of resident state on hardware with 192 GiB per device, which is why sharding is arithmetic rather than preference.
Ring all-reduce moves 2(P-1)/P x S per rank, converging to 2S. Volume is independent of scale; step count is not.
Tensor parallel costs 4 all-reduces per layer against data parallel's one per step, which is why TP stays inside a node.

modules.title: Problem framing and metrics
modules.one_liner: The system produces a decision, not a prediction.

bullets.text: Name the action and the good outcome before the model. Metrics are proxies; the threshold comes from the relative cost of each error type.

modules.title: Data pipelines and features
modules.one_liner: The data pipeline is the system; the architecture rarely is.

bullets.text: Label leakage makes the offline metric a fiction, not merely optimistic.
Training-serving skew comes from computing one feature in two code paths. The fix is one path.

modules.title: Training systems
modules.one_liner: A distributed system with a loss function attached.

bullets.text: Uptime is decided by the input pipeline, bit-exact resumable checkpoints, and dead-rank detection time - none of which are modelling concerns.

modules.title: Production model optimization
modules.one_liner: Cheapest and least risky first, in a fixed order.

bullets.text: Do not call the model, then serve it better, then shrink the numbers, then shrink the model. Distillation is late for a reason.

modules.title: Deployment and serving architecture
modules.one_liner: Scale on queue depth, not utilization.

bullets.text: Pick the serving pattern from latency, cost, freshness, connectivity and privacy. Online, async, streaming, batch and edge are different systems.
Put the model behind its own service so it can scale and ship independently of the application.

modules.title: Monitoring, drift and ethics
modules.one_liner: Perfectly healthy and quietly wrong is a real state.

bullets.text: Monitor system, data, model and business layers; alert on very few of them.
Covariate shift and label shift have different causes and different fixes; naming which one you have is most of the work.

modules.title: Capstone case studies
modules.one_liner: Design is constraint arithmetic, practised end to end.

bullets.text: Two worked designs: LLM serving and a recommender, each with the goal, latency budget, traffic forecast and price list made explicit.
Say which constraint you would break first. An architecture that satisfies all four without a stated tradeoff is usually under-specified.

modules.title: Scaling limits and communication cost
modules.one_liner: Processors add capacity; only independence turns capacity into speed.

bullets.text: Amdahl caps a fixed problem at 1/s speedup; Gustafson escapes it by growing the problem. Neither includes communication.
Add the alpha-beta term and the curve turns over rather than plateauing: past some rank count more ranks are slower.

modules.title: Message passing with MPI
modules.one_liner: The model you get once you accept there is no shared memory.

bullets.text: A process knows only its own rank and its group size, and can affect another only by a message the other explicitly agrees to receive.
This module's C sources are the one exception in the repo that was actually compiled: warning-free under -Wall -Wextra against Open MPI 5.0.10 headers. Compiled, not run.

modules.title: GPU collectives (NCCL and RCCL)
modules.one_liner: Turning different gradients into the same averaged gradient, as fast as the wires allow.

bullets.text: NCCL and RCCL are API-compatible siblings: same call sequence, same environment variables, largely the same algorithms.
Ring all-reduce byte count converges (1.75m at N=8, 1.998m at N=1024) while the step count stays linear (14 steps against 2,046).

modules.title: Interconnects and RDMA
modules.one_liner: Five tiers, each about an order of magnitude from the next.

bullets.text: On-package memory, scale-up links, PCIe, scale-out network, storage. The ladder explains why tensor parallelism stays inside a node.

modules.title: Topology and scale boundaries
modules.one_liner: A cluster is a shape, and the shape decides which links you may use at once.

bullets.text: Diameter sets the latency term, bisection bandwidth sets the throughput term. Those two numbers characterize any topology.

modules.title: Real systems at scale
modules.one_liner: The reference machines differ in processors and hardly at all in reasoning.

bullets.text: Frontier, El Capitan, Aurora, Fugaku, Summit and LUMI each spend their design budget on moving data.
Which constraint binds changes by decade of rank count, which is what the scale-boundary infographic plots.

analogies.world: A stadium of 50,000 diligent students, against a handful of geniuses
analogies.machine: thousands of GPU threads running one kernel, against a few CPU cores

analogies.world: A warehouse across town, a truck that leaves full either way, and a workbench inside the building
analogies.machine: global memory, one memory transaction, and shared memory / LDS

analogies.world: A rowing eight: one call from the cox, every oar together
analogies.machine: a warp of 32 or a wavefront of 64 executing one instruction in lockstep
analogies.breaks: Lanes are not people. Masking one costs nothing but the lost slot, and NVIDIA Volta and later give lanes their own program counters.

analogies.world: The stadium pairs off, adds, and half of them sit down each round
analogies.machine: the reduction tree: same work, log2(n) depth
analogies.breaks: Anyone can pair with anyone in a stadium. On a GPU two threads exchange cheaply only inside a warp or a block; across blocks there is no cheap handshake.

analogies.world: A bank statement's running balance, with a clerk on every line instead of one walking down the page
analogies.machine: parallel prefix sum, Hillis-Steele or Blelloch
analogies.breaks: Rounds need a barrier: nobody may start round 2 until every clerk finished round 1, so the slowest lane sets the pace.

analogies.world: Checking a stack of books out to a table your study group shares, instead of walking to the shelf per number
analogies.machine: shared-memory tiling, so each loaded element feeds T FMAs
analogies.breaks: Three places, each a real GPU constraint the library has no analogue for.

analogies.world: Grading on a curve, subtracting the top score first so no number overflows the calculator
analogies.machine: numerically safe softmax with the row maximum removed
analogies.breaks: An examiner reads the whole class list before deciding the top score. A GPU wants to avoid re-reading the list at all, because reading is the expensive part.

analogies.world: One work order for a whole crew, instead of briefing every worker individually
analogies.machine: a Triton program operating on a block of elements
analogies.breaks: The dispatcher is not clairvoyant: a badly sized work order is still slow, and you fix it by rewriting the order, not by micromanaging a worker.

analogies.world: Totalling a ledger without ever printing the spreadsheet
analogies.machine: FlashAttention: the score tile is computed, used and discarded on chip
analogies.breaks: One clerk, thousands of desks. The real kernel runs thousands of programs, each owning a block of rows, so there is no single sequential pass.

analogies.world: Standard shipping containers and stacking rules, instead of an instruction card per parcel
analogies.machine: CuTe layouts and CUTLASS collectives
analogies.breaks: Containers are inert; an MMA atom is not. It specifies which thread holds which element in which register, so it is a data layout and a thread layout at once.

analogies.world: A factory floor: production lines, a toolbox at each station, a workbench beside the line
analogies.machine: CUs or SMs, registers, and LDS or shared memory
analogies.breaks: A factory worker can wait; a GPU lane cannot. Lanes run in lockstep, so the machine hides latency by switching whole waves rather than by letting one worker pause.

analogies.world: A restaurant kitchen where the chef is faster than the delivery van
analogies.machine: a memory-bound kernel: attainable = min(peak, intensity x bandwidth)
analogies.breaks: It assumes a steady stream of orders. For a single tiny kernel the dominant cost is launch overhead, and the roofline is silent about that regime entirely.

analogies.world: The doctor who takes a history and orders one decisive test, not every scan in the catalogue
analogies.machine: profiling as a decision procedure: hypothesis first, cheapest disconfirming measurement second
analogies.breaks: The scan changes the patient. Counter collection can serialize and replay kernel dispatches, distorting precisely the small fast kernels you most wanted to measure.

analogies.world: A ruler: which unit it measures in, and how many ticks sit between units
analogies.machine: the exponent buys range; the mantissa buys precision
analogies.breaks: A real ruler has uniformly spaced ticks. A float re-scales its ticks at every power of two, which is why 1000000.0 + 0.01 can equal 1000000.0 exactly.

analogies.world: The banquet order against the single a la carte plate, in a kitchen with a long pantry corridor
analogies.machine: prefill against decode: compute-bound against bandwidth-bound
analogies.breaks: Stated in the module: three places, each worth knowing.

analogies.world: A restaurant that will not seat anyone new until every diner at the communal table has left
analogies.machine: static batching, and why continuous batching replaces it
analogies.breaks: Diners do not slow each other down; sequences do. Every admitted sequence adds work to every step, so each new guest makes all current guests eat slower.

analogies.world: Identical building crews who meet on an evening call to merge one day's blueprint edits
analogies.machine: data parallelism, and the gradient all-reduce
analogies.breaks: Crews tolerate disagreement; gradients cannot. Two houses a millimetre apart are both fine, but two ranks whose parameters differ produce a divergent model.

analogies.world: Hiring one engineer from 500 applicants: hiring someone bad against rejecting someone great
analogies.machine: precision against recall, and where you set the threshold
analogies.breaks: Capacity, not cost, often sets the real threshold. A cost-optimal threshold assumes you can act on every alert, and a queue with twelve analysts cannot.

analogies.world: A practice test with the answer key printed on the back of every page
analogies.machine: label leakage, and the offline metric it invents
analogies.breaks: The exam tells you your real score; production often does not. Online labels are noisy and delayed, so the fiction can survive far longer than one exam day.

analogies.world: A long road trip in a car that breaks down, stopping at towns to write down where you are
analogies.machine: checkpoint interval derived from failure rate and checkpoint cost
analogies.breaks: A synchronous training job has no independent cars. One rank failing kills all of them, so the failure rate scales with GPU count while useful work per GPU does not.

analogies.world: Cutting a household energy bill: lights off, then the door seal, then LEDs, and only then the walls
analogies.machine: the optimization ladder, ordered by cost, risk and reversibility
analogies.breaks: A light switch cannot damage the house; a model change can damage the product. Every rung below 'serve it better' alters what the model outputs.

analogies.world: Opening a new bridge: test trucks first, then one lane, then everyone
analogies.machine: shadow traffic, then a canary with automated rollback
analogies.breaks: A bridge does not learn from its own traffic. Your model's outputs shape the data that trains its successor.

analogies.world: A smoke detector against an annual check-up
analogies.machine: the service dashboard against model monitoring
analogies.breaks: A check-up has a reference range; your model does not. Whether a prediction mean of 0.31 is healthy depends on last month's 0.28 and on whether the world moved.

analogies.world: An emergency department: 90 seconds of triage for everyone, cheap tests for many, the scanner for a few
analogies.machine: a cascade architecture sized for the bad Saturday night
analogies.breaks: A triage nurse does not get better at triage because of who she admitted last week. An ML system trains on its own outputs, so it has a feedback loop a hospital does not.

analogies.world: Painting a very long fence: one painter 100 hours, ten painters about ten
analogies.machine: Amdahl's ceiling, Gustafson's escape, and the communication term neither includes
analogies.breaks: Passing paint samples is O(1) per painter, so the meeting looks like a headcount problem. A real all-reduce moves a fixed volume; what grows with rank count is the step count.

analogies.world: Researchers in sealed offices, passing notes through a slot in the door
analogies.machine: MPI: private address spaces, explicit send and matching receive
analogies.breaks: The corridor outbox is optional and invisible. Implementations buffer small messages eagerly, so a 100-byte send returns at once while a 100 MB send blocks for a rendezvous.

analogies.world: Twenty-four people in a circle passing batons, instead of everyone shouting at everyone
analogies.machine: ring all-reduce: reduce-scatter then all-gather
analogies.breaks: The circle is not a circle. Links inside a server are an order of magnitude faster than the network between them, so a real library orders its ring to cross expensive hops rarely.

analogies.world: An office building: adjacent desks, then other floors, then a courier to another site
analogies.machine: the tier ladder from registers to HBM to scale-up links to the network
analogies.breaks: The tiers differ in kind, not only in speed. A peer GPU's memory in the scale-up domain is addressable by an ordinary load; nothing across the network is.

analogies.world: Three honest ways to build a road network between a thousand towns
analogies.machine: fat-tree, dragonfly and torus, each with a diameter and a bisection
analogies.breaks: Roads have no credits. A lossless fabric does not drop packets, it pushes back, and that backpressure travels upstream to flows that were never congested.

analogies.world: A very large restaurant kitchen, where past some size the limit stops being the cooking
analogies.machine: real systems at scale, where the design budget goes to moving data
analogies.breaks: Kitchens degrade gracefully; a tightly-coupled job does not. It runs at the speed of its worst participant, and when one dies the whole job dies with it.
